content: CD93, also known as Cluster of Differentiation 93, is a protein encoded by the CD93 gene in humans. It is a C-type lectin transmembrane receptor that is involved in processes such as cell-cell adhesion and host defense mechanisms. CD93 is a member of the Group XIV C-type lectin family, which also includes endosialin (CD248), CLEC14A, and thrombomodulin, a well-characterized anticoagulant. Proteins in this family share structural features, including a C-type lectin domain, multiple epidermal growth factor-like domains, a highly glycosylated mucin-like domain, a unique transmembrane domain, and a short cytoplasmic tail. Due to its strong homology with thrombomodulin and their close proximity on chromosome 20, CD93 is thought to have originated from the thrombomodulin gene through a duplication event. Initially, CD93 was identified on an early population of hematopoietic stem cells, which give rise to all mature blood cells. It is now known to be expressed on a variety of cell types, including platelets, monocytes, microglia, and endothelial cells. Within the immune system, CD93 is expressed on neutrophils, activated macrophages, B cell precursors (up to the T2 stage in the spleen), a subset of dendritic cells, and natural killer cells. Molecular studies have revealed that CD93 is identical to C1qRp, a human protein initially identified as a putative receptor for C1q. C1q is a complement activation protein that plays a critical role in the classical complement pathway, leading to the formation of the membrane attack complex. C1q is also involved in other immunological processes, such as enhancing bacterial phagocytosis, clearing apoptotic cells, and neutralizing viruses. Interestingly, anti-C1qRp antibodies have been shown to significantly reduce C1q-enhanced phagocytosis. However, more recent studies have confirmed that while CD93 and C1qRp are the same protein, there is no direct interaction between CD93 and C1q under physiological conditions. CD93 is re-expressed during late B cell differentiation and can serve as a marker for plasma cell maturation. It has been found to be differentially expressed in grade IV glioma vasculature compared to low-grade gliomas or normal brain tissue, with high expression correlating with poor patient survival. Functionally, CD93 was initially thought to act as a receptor for C1q but is now believed to play a role in intercellular adhesion and the clearance of apoptotic cells. The intracellular cytoplasmic tail of CD93 contains two highly conserved domains, one of which interacts with moesin, a protein involved in linking transmembrane proteins to the cytoskeleton and remodeling the cytoskeleton. This interaction is crucial for adhesion, migration, and phagocytosis, all of which are functions in which CD93 is implicated. In the context of late B cell differentiation, CD93 is essential for maintaining high antibody titers after immunization and for the survival of long-lived plasma cells in the bone marrow. CD93-deficient mice fail to sustain high antibody levels following immunization and exhibit reduced numbers of antigen-specific plasma cells in the bone marrow. In endothelial cells, CD93 is involved in cell-cell adhesion, cell spreading, migration, polarization, and tubular morphogenesis. Recent findings indicate that CD93 regulates endothelial cell dynamics through its interaction with the extracellular matrix glycoprotein MMRN2. The absence of CD93 or MMRN2 in endothelial cells disrupts fibronectin fibrillogenesis and decreases integrin β1 activation. CD93 also plays a significant role in glioma development. Glioma-bearing CD93 knockout mice exhibit smaller tumor sizes and improved survival. These tumors show disrupted fibronectin fibrillogenesis and reduced integrin β1 activation, highlighting the importance of CD93 in tumor progression.
